title: Derivative filtering
physicalPurpose: Retain useful derivative damping without converting encoder noise into excessive motor-torque activity.
principalTechnique: First- and second-order low-pass filtering before derivative action
objective: Select a derivative-filter time constant and order from measured noise attenuation and lag.

simplifications: Seeded additive white encoder noise has constant 0.002 rad standard deviation.
Gravity torque is 4*sin(theta) N m; 4 N m is its peak coefficient, not a constant load.
The rigid table omits flexible resonance; later frequency-domain lessons test resonance explicitly.

baseline.limitation: Derivative on the noisy raw encoder produces excessive scan-to-scan motor-torque changes.

change.decision: Require torque-increment RMS at or below 0.250 N m and positive lag area at or below 0.020 rad s; among qualifying candidates choose the simplest filter and then the smallest time constant.

disturbances: Seeded encoder measurement noise throughout every run

abortPredicates: Raw position, filtered position, velocity or torque is nonfinite
Applied torque leaves -10 to 10 N m
safety.restorationMode: Manual with zero torque after mechanically supporting the payload
simulationOnlyRestrictions: Seeded simulation noise does not qualify a physical encoder, flexible resonance or drive current spectrum.

video.viewerOutcome: Explain derivative noise amplification and select a low-pass filter from measured torque attenuation and lag rather than smooth appearance.

learning.context: The loaded positioning table now reports a seeded noisy encoder signal while PID retains derivative on measurement.
learning.reason: Lesson 22 removed setpoint kick, but derivative action still reacts to every measured encoder change, including noise that is not physical motion.
theory: Measurement noise is unwanted variation added to the encoder reading. Its standard deviation sigma is 0.002 rad in this deterministic experiment.
A finite-difference derivative divides each measurement change by cycle time dt, so shorter dt and high-frequency noise can create large torque changes through Kd.

A low-pass filter creates controller-facing position y_f that follows slow position changes while attenuating fast changes. Its time constant tau controls cutoff: larger tau removes more fast motion but delays the measurement more. Filter order states how many identical stages are cascaded.

The update coefficient a equals dt divided by tau plus one half dt. Each stage adds a times the difference between its input and previous output; the second-order candidate applies the same stage twice.

Torque-increment RMS is the square root of the mean squared successive applied-torque changes from 15 to 20 s. Positive position-lag area sums positive raw-position minus controller-position differences times dt from 0 to 5 s. Filtering should reduce the first measure while increasing the second.
learning.workedPrediction: With dt 0.02 s and tau 0.05 s, coefficient a is 0.333. A 0.003 rad raw-minus-filtered difference moves a first-order output by 0.001 rad in one scan; a second stage smooths it again but adds lag.
practicalPreparation: Confirm identical 0.5 rad step, 20 ms cycle, 0.002 rad seeded noise, angle-dependent 4*sin(theta) N m gravity, torque limits, initial state and seed for every run.
learning.baseline: Bypass filtering, retain raw and controller-facing PV plus applied torque, and calculate late torque-increment RMS and early positive lag area.
learning.change: Run the first-order filter at 0.02, 0.05 and 0.10 s while changing only its time constant. Then compare first- and second-order filtering at the selected 0.05 s time constant.
learning.comparison: Compare noise visible in raw and controller-facing PV, late torque-increment RMS, early positive lag area, final-window tracking and torque limits on equal scales.
learning.validation: Require each added order to reduce torque-increment RMS to at most 80 percent of the preceding case, lag area to increase strictly with order, 18 to 20 s mean controller position within 0.02 rad of SP, finite values and applied torque within plus or minus 10 N m.
learning.explanation: Explain why filtering removes high-frequency measurement content before differentiation but delays the controller's view of real motion; a smoother trace is not free information.
learning.transfer: Choose derivative filtering from sensor spectrum, sample time, plant bandwidth and resonance risk; Lesson 24 introduces mechanical nonidealities that filtering and retuning cannot repair.
